title: Increasing Future Global Compound Heat Flash Droughts and Socioeconomic Exposure
content:
Abstract

Compound heat flash droughts (CHFDs) can severely impact human society. However, the spatiotemporal evolution and socioeconomic impacts under future scenarios remain poorly understood. Here, we conduct a global assessment of spatiotemporal patterns and socioeconomic exposure of CHFDs using reanalysis data (1950–2024) and future projections from eight climate models under three scenarios. Under SSP2-4.5, CHFD frequency increases across over two-thirds of the global land area, with a mean increase of 0.22 events per decade. In the long-term future (2071–2100), high-frequency CHFDs are concentrated in northwestern South America (NWS), the South American monsoon (SAM) region, and Southeast Asia (SEA), whereas stronger severity is most pronounced in mid- to high-latitude regions, such as western Siberia. The frequency in NWS reaches approximately 20 events per decade under SSP2-4.5, nearly 4.3 times the historical level. Under SSP2-4.5, population and gross domestic product (GDP) exposure reach 49.23% and 48.29%, respectively, by the early 2090s (i.e., 0.49 and 0.48 events per capita and per unit of GDP), whereas NWS, SAM, SEA, and Madagascar together account for approximately 26.5% of global exposure in the long-term future. Decomposition reveals that changes in future socioeconomic exposure are dominated by the climate effect. Upper-middle-income regions exhibit the highest socioeconomic exposure, followed by low-income regions. In the long-term future, population and GDP exposure in upper-middle-income regions are more than twice those in high-income regions. Our findings indicate intensifying socioeconomic impacts of CHFDs, coupled with widening regional disparities, underscoring the need for region-specific adaptation and risk-management strategies, especially in emerging economies.
